desc: Students submit a final software project alongside a comprehensive prompt log. They are assessed on how they iteratively broke down complex problems into discrete prompts, how they corrected AI hallucinations, and how they stitched AI-generated modules together.

method: Code Review & Refactor of AI output
desc: Instructors generate a deliberately flawed codebase using GenAI containing security vulnerabilities, inefficiencies, or similar. Students must act as QA engineers identifying the flaws, writing a critical review, and refactoring the code to meet industry standards.
Students use AI to generate a baseline system architecture for a standard problem. They must then write a critical report identifying the AI's scaling bottlenecks or errors.

The student must modify an AI generated design to fit a highly specific edge-case constraint. This is typically employed as a two part assessment in a continuous assessment mode. 1) student uses AI to generate the architecture/code; 2) the student is given a brief to modify the constraints in a short period of time.

Students write a solution to a complex algorithm manually, then prompt an AI to write a solution for the same task. The assessment requires the student to benchmark both approaches for time complexity, memory allocation, and readability.

Students use AI to generate the source code for a complex application. The students task is to act as a QA engineer, writing comprehensive, adversarial tests designed specifically to break the AI code or expose unhandled edge cases.

Provide students with a functional but outdated codebase, then students must use AI to migrate the system to a modern framework and write a report detailing how they verified that the AI maintained the original logic and improved performance.

Provide the students with a highly specific, complex, or stylistically unique piece of working code generated by AI, the students must reverse-engineer the prompt, constraints, and context window that were required to generate that exact output, proving they understand the underlying structure of the code.
Students build a project using an AI coding assistant but they must record instances where the AI suggested incorrect logic, explain why the AI made that specific error, and how they intervened.
Students prompt an AI to build a sensitive application which they must then conduct a formal ethical and bias audit and patch the vulnerabilities.

Students are graded heavily on their Git commit history rather than the product. They must demonstrate a logical, incremental evolution of their codebase. Sudden, massive commits of perfect code are flagged. The assessment values human development.
Instructors provide the architecture and unit tests where students strictly write the core algorithmic logic to make tests pass.
Instructors design a brief tied to a local, fictional, or highly unique dataset/hardware setup that AI lacks training data on.
Students maintain a weekly log documenting specific bugs encountered, what they prompted, where AI failed, and the solution.
Mid-way through a project, alter an API schema or inject a bug into the supporting software then students must diagnose the breaking change and adapt it.
Students write the architecture manually (e.g. interfaces, endpoints). Once submitted, they use AI to generate boilerplate implementation.
Students submit AI-assisted code with very detailed inline annotations explaining memory management, execution flow, and time complexity.
Code is evaluated by an automated grading server against a large suite of hidden, highly complex edge cases.
Students draft formal software specifications from a vague client brief.
Students translate language-agnostic pseudocode into formal code.
A short live interview where students are asked dynamic questions about a submitted piece of work.
Students complete a coding task in a secure, offline computer lab with only an IDE and local docs.
In an invigilated setting, students are provided with a broken piece of code and a trace. They must find and fix the bug under a time limit.
Students present working software live to an instructor, running edge-case inputs on the spot.
Students enter an offline lab with their previously submitted coursework and have to add one new feature.
Students draw a system architecture (e.g., database schema, APIs) on a physical whiteboard in 20 minutes while answering questions.
The student’s code must interact with physical lab hardware.
Groups of three students critique each other's code live in a room without internet access.
Traditional written exam
